players.name: Kristaps Porzingis
players.outlook: Porzingis is one of the elite per-minute producers of his generation, but injuries have consistently derailed his availability and is already out for training camp. Porzingis missed 50 games last season and 40 the season before, and has missed at least 16 games in nine straight seasons. He is slotted to be the Warriors' starting center this season, and when he plays he will produce, but he is risky to draft in fantasy leagues before the late-middle rounds at the earliest.

players.name: Jalen Williams
players.outlook: Williams is coming off an injury-riddled season in which he was only able to play 33 games at a career-low 28.4 MPG. After an offseason to get healthy, Williams is expected to bounce back to or even surpass the rounded 22 points, 5 rebounds, 5 assists and 2 combined blocks and steals he posted in 2024-25. Still only 25 years old and playing next to Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Chet Holmgren, Williams should still be getting better every season.

players.name: CJ McCollum
players.outlook: McCollum was traded to the Hawks at midseason and fit in perfectly with the rest of their lineup in 2025-26. More shooter-scorer lead guard than true point guard, McCollum works with backcourt-mate Nickeil Alexander-Walker to generate points and scoring opportunities for teammates while playing off Jalen Johnson. Fantasy-wise, McCollum's scoring, 3-point shooting, assists and rebounds make him a top-80 fantasy prospect.

players.name: Tobias Harris
players.outlook: Harris enters the season competing with Julian Champagnie for the Spurs starting power forward job. He averaged 13.3 PPG and 5.1 RPG in 63 games for the Pistons last season, then raised his production to 18.1 PPG and 7.2 RPG in the playoffs. Harris brings shooting, rebounding and the ability to create his own shot, but San Antonio’s deep rotation could limit his usage. Winning the starting job would give him a clearer path to fantasy value. Given the circumstances, Harris is worth taking a flier on later in drafts.

The upside is clear, with Edey offering double-double production, strong rebounding and blocks. The concern is durability after another foot surgery. If healthy, Edey has room to take another statistical jump.

longterm.name: Aaron Gordon
longterm.outlook: Gordon enters this season looking to stay healthy after injuries limited him to just 36 games last season. He averaged 16.2 PPG, 5.8 RPG and 2.7 APG while shooting 49.7% from the field. Gordon can provide efficient scoring, rebounds and some three-point production, but durability has become a concern after he played only 51 games the previous season. He’s best viewed as a late-round bench stash, with his value tied closely to how many games he can stay on the floor.

longterm.name: Rudy Gobert
longterm.outlook: Gobert has been a model of consistency on defense and the glass for a decade. For the last two seasons, Gobert had been part of a triumverate of impact big men with Julius Randle and Naz Reid. This offseason, the Timberwolves traded Randle to the Nets and Reid to the Hornets without getting a starting caliber big in either deal. This solidifies Gobert with as many minutes as he can handle, so he seems poised for one of his stronger campaigns.

longterm.name: Peyton Watson
longterm.outlook: Watson arrives in Cleveland after a breakout season in Denver. He averaged career highs of 14.6 PPG, 4.9 RPG and 1.1 BPG while shooting 41.1% from beyond the arc, but his upside really showed when Nikola Jokic was out. Watson averaged 22.1 PPG, 5.8 RPG and 2.3 triples per game. A hamstring injury ended his season. With starter-level minutes expected in Cleveland, Watson is an intriguing late-round target with room to take another statistical jump.

Though his averages are not eye-popping, he contributes positively across-the-board without any negatives, adding to his value in category leagues.

Still, Champagnie is more of a waiver-wire option in most leagues, with his fantasy value likely to rise if he holds onto the starting job.
